Zimbabwe’s Metals & Mining Sector Attracts Fresh Investment in Major Expansion Drive

Zimbabwe’s metals and mining industry is set for a significant boost as new investments pour into the sector, with local and foreign firms announcing ambitious expansion plans aimed at ramping up production of strategic minerals.

The latest development comes as ZimMet Resources, a Harare-based mining company, confirmed on Wednesday that it would invest $220 million over the next three years to expand operations at its flagship nickel and chrome mines in the Midlands Province. The expansion is expected to increase the company’s annual nickel production capacity by 35% and create over 600 direct jobs.

“We are committed to supporting Zimbabwe’s vision of becoming a key global supplier of critical minerals,” said Tendai Mupfuti, CEO of ZimMet Resources. “Our investment will not only boost export earnings but also foster skills development and value addition in the country.”

The announcement follows a series of similar commitments in recent months, as the government’s drive to attract capital and modernize the sector gains traction. The Ministry of Mines and Mining Development reported that total pledged investments in the industry have reached $1.1 billion in the past twelve months, with projects spanning lithium, gold, platinum, and rare earth exploration.

Industry analysts attribute the surge in interest to Zimbabwe’s extensive mineral reserves and ongoing reforms aimed at improving the investment climate. “There is a clear policy shift towards transparency and investor protection,” said Miriam Chikowore, a mining analyst at Harare-based consultancy StratMet Advisory. “Coupled with improved infrastructure and a skilled workforce, Zimbabwe is becoming increasingly attractive for mining investment.”

Trade unions welcomed the expansion, noting the potential for job creation and community development. “We urge companies to prioritize local employment and ensure compliance with environmental and safety standards,” said Peter Sibanda, spokesperson for the National Mine Workers Union of Zimbabwe.

According to data from the Zimbabwe Chamber of Mines, the sector currently accounts for 60% of the country’s export earnings and employs over 90,000 people. The government aims to boost mineral exports to $12 billion by 2025, up from $5.7 billion in 2023, as part of its national development agenda.

However, analysts note that infrastructure bottlenecks and access to reliable power remain challenges for the sector’s growth. The government has pledged further investments in road, rail, and energy projects to support the mining boom.

With new capital inflows and ongoing policy reforms, Zimbabwe’s metals and mining industry appears poised for sustained growth, reinforcing its role as a cornerstone of the national economy.
